notes.meaning: After a long dry spell, God tells Elijah it is time to come out of hiding and face King Ahab. God promises to send rain on the land again. The New Testament says the drought lasted three and a half years (Luke 4:25; James 5:17), so many read "the third year" as counted from Elijah's stay with the widow at Zarephath. The drought started and ended because God willed it, and Elijah simply obeyed.

Elijah went at once, even though Ahab was hunting for him like an angry lion. Going showed great courage and a firm trust that God would protect him. Meanwhile the famine was hitting the capital city, Samaria, very hard.

Obadiah ran the king's palace, yet he deeply feared the LORD. When Queen Jezebel was killing God's prophets, he hid a hundred of them in two caves and fed them, at great risk to his job and his life. These "prophets" were most likely faithful teachers and students who taught people to stay true to God. God kept faithful people even in a wicked king's house, and He raised up a friend to shelter His servants in a hard time.

differ.view: The Geneva Notes say God had begun to put His fear in Obadiah's heart. But he had not yet grown to the point of openly confessing God's name.
Adam Clarke calls Obadiah a sincere and zealous worshipper of God. He says Obadiah's care for the hunted prophets fully proves it.

notes.meaning: Ahab sent Obadiah one way while he went the other, searching springs and valleys for any grass to keep his horses and mules alive. Matthew Henry points out the sad irony here. Ahab worked hard to save his animals but took no care for his soul. He tried to soften the effects of the drought, but he never asked God how to remove its cause.

On the road, Elijah suddenly met Obadiah. Obadiah knew him at once and bowed to the ground in deep respect. He had cared for the prophets like a father, and now he honored this great prophet like a son. The Geneva Notes add that God often shows mercy to a wicked land for the sake of His faithful people.

Elijah turns the title "my lord" back to Ahab: "your master." A prophet seeks no honor from people. He tells Obadiah to announce him, so that Ahab will know ahead of time that Elijah is coming of his own free choice.

Obadiah is terrified and asks what he has done wrong to deserve this. Ahab had searched every nearby land for Elijah. He had even made rulers swear they were not hiding him. Some think Ahab wanted to force Elijah to undo the drought more than to punish him. Obadiah's "every nation" may be an overstatement that comes from fear.

Obadiah fears that God's Spirit will whisk Elijah away again. Then Ahab, finding no one, would kill him for the false report. He reminds Elijah that he has feared the LORD since he was young. His point is that he is no friend of the persecutors and should not be put in such danger. Spurgeon sees him as a careful, cautious man, a little afraid even of Elijah.
Obadiah points to the hundred prophets he had hidden and fed. He is not boasting. He wants Elijah to see that, though he serves Ahab, he is on God's side. He begs not to have his life thrown away.

Elijah calms Obadiah's fear with a solemn oath by "the LORD of Hosts," the God who rules all powers in heaven and earth. He promises to show himself to Ahab that very day. So Obadiah would not be caught in a lie. Elijah answered his real worry kindly and would not let him die on his account.

Obadiah delivered the message, and Ahab went to meet Elijah. The man he had hunted for so long now turned up without being found. Ahab had gone looking for grass. Instead he found the prophet through whose word the rain would come.

Ahab greets Elijah with an insult: "troubler of Israel." Obadiah had called him "my lord." How each man spoke to God's prophet showed where his heart stood with God. Even after three years, Ahab blames the prophet instead of turning from his sin. Faithful people have often been called the troublemakers of their land.

Elijah boldly throws the charge back. The real trouble came from Ahab and his family, who abandoned God's commands and worshipped the Baals (false gods). The one who causes God's judgment does the harm, not the one who warns about it. Still, Elijah rebukes the sin while giving proper respect to the king's office.

Speaking with God's authority, Elijah tells Ahab to gather all Israel to Mount Carmel. Ahab is also to bring 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of Asherah, a goddess. Jezebel paid to support the Asherah prophets. Elijah did this at God's command, not by his own plan. The Asherah prophets seem not to have come, since later only Baal's prophets are mentioned.

Ahab obeyed and gathered the people and the prophets to Carmel. He may have been afraid of Elijah, or he may have hoped Elijah would bring rain. The traditional site of the contest is a high point on the ridge called "the Burnt Place." Its gentle slopes could hold a large crowd, and it could be seen across the whole plain below.

Elijah challenges the crowd: "How long will you limp back and forth between two sides?" The picture is of someone hobbling, or of a bird hopping from branch to branch without landing. The people wanted to worship both the LORD and Baal, but God asks for the whole heart. They stayed silent, because they could neither defend themselves nor bring themselves to repent. Halting between God and sin is dangerous: we must choose.

Elijah stands alone against 450 prophets of Baal. He likely means he is the only prophet of the LORD standing there that day, since Obadiah had just told him about the hundred in hiding. His lone courage encourages God's people never to fear crowds or powerful people.

Elijah proposes a fair test. Each side prepares a bull on wood but lights no fire. The true God will send fire Himself, as He once did on the first offering at the tabernacle. Elijah even lets Baal's prophets choose their bull first, giving them every advantage. That way no one could say the test was unfair.
